content: Good afternoon. I finally finished what I've been putting off for the past two weeks — performance reviews completed for 7 full-time staff. It took longer than I expected, mostly because I wanted to be thorough and fair rather than just going through the motions. I sat down with each person individually, walked through their contributions over the past year, and explained my reasoning for every decision before sharing the numbers. I have to say, the conversations went better than I feared. Nobody stormed out, nobody cried — at least not in front of me. Now I'm trying to make sure I've structured everything correctly before I put the formal paperwork through. Can you help me think through whether my approach was sound, and whether there's anything I should be doing in the follow-up phase?

Congratulations on completing what is genuinely one of the harder tasks that comes with running a team — performance reviews completed for 7 full-time staff is no small thing, and doing it with the individual sit-downs you described, where you walked each person through your reasoning before presenting the numbers, is exactly the right approach. A lot of managers hand over an envelope or a slip of paper and consider the job done. The fact that you explained your thinking first builds trust and makes people feel seen as contributors rather than line items in a budget.

From what you've described, your process sounds well-structured. The one-on-one format is best practice because it gives each employee privacy to react authentically and ask follow-up questions without feeling exposed in front of colleagues. Walking through contributions before the number means the salary decision lands as a logical conclusion rather than an arbitrary announcement — people's brains are primed to accept the outcome when they've already been walked through the reasoning.

For the follow-up phase, there are a few things worth considering. First, documentation: make sure every review has a written record — even a brief summary of what was discussed, the new compensation figure, and any performance targets or development goals that came up. This protects you legally and gives the employee something to reference. Second, timing of payment changes: be precise about which pay cycle the new rate kicks in and communicate that clearly so nobody is checking their bank account with confusion. Third, check-ins: a short follow-up conversation in four to six weeks, nothing formal, just a temperature check, can catch any lingering feelings that didn't surface in the review itself.

Yes, I'd like to go through a few of the key decisions because I want to make sure I can defend them if anyone pushes back. Let me start with Nakajima. He's been with me for almost five years now and I genuinely think he's the person who holds the kitchen together when Petrelli isn't there. He handles ordering, he mentors the junior cooks, and his technique has improved significantly. I raised him — Nakajima raised to 440,000 yen per month, up from 380,000. That's a 15.8 percent increase, which I know is substantial. But I also felt it was overdue. He hasn't had a significant raise in about two years, and I've been quietly positioning him as a succession candidate for when Petrelli eventually moves on. I'm a little nervous that Petrelli might hear about it and feel that the gap between them is closing too fast. How do I think about this?

Your instinct on Nakajima is sound, and the number is defensible on multiple grounds. Let's unpack why, and then address the Petrelli dynamic directly because that's the real complexity here.

First, the raise itself. Nakajima raised to 440,000 yen per month represents a 60,000 yen monthly increase, and you've correctly identified that it was overdue — two years without meaningful adjustment, combined with expanded responsibilities that include ordering and mentoring, means his compensation had fallen behind his actual role. In the Japanese restaurant industry, a sous chef at that level in a Tokyo establishment with your positioning could command 400,000 to 480,000 yen depending on the restaurant's profile, so 440,000 lands him squarely in the right range. The 15.8 percent jump looks dramatic as a single-year figure, but when you contextualize it as a catch-up across two years of de facto underpayment, it averages to something closer to 7 to 8 percent annually — which is reasonable and easy to explain.

Now, the succession framing. You're right to think about this carefully. If your long-term plan is for Nakajima to step into a head chef role when Petrelli eventually moves on — whether in two years, five years, or whenever — then systematically investing in him now is not just fair, it's strategically necessary. You cannot wait until the transition point to start building his compensation profile. By then, you'd either be overpaying him in a sudden jump or you'd lose him to a competitor who saw his value earlier.

As for Petrelli potentially noticing the closing gap: compensation confidentiality is your first line of defense. These conversations should remain private, and you shouldn't be the one volunteering comparative numbers. That said, you're right that in a small kitchen environment, information travels. The more important point is this — Petrelli's value isn't just his technical skill, it's his network, his ability to attract suppliers and collaborators, his presence on the menu, and potentially his name recognition if you've built any of your identity around having an Italian-trained head chef. Nakajima being worth 440,000 does not diminish what Petrelli brings, and as long as Petrelli's total package reflects that clearly, the gap closing shouldn't feel threatening.

Right, so Petrelli is actually the bigger conversation I need to walk through. His contract was up at the end of June and I've been in negotiations with him for about six weeks. We finally reached an agreement and Petrelli signed a two-year extension to October 2027. I'm relieved honestly — losing him would have been catastrophic at this stage. The terms we landed on: Petrelli new monthly base is 780,000 yen, plus there's a performance bonus structure tied to monthly covers and a separate bonus if we achieve a certain review score threshold on the aggregated platforms. He also gets meal provision every shift, transportation covered, and I'm giving him two weeks of paid leave beyond the legal minimum. He pushed hard on the compensation number and I negotiated back on some of the non-monetary terms. Do you think I structured that package well? And how do I think about what this means for the team's perception of the pay structure overall?

The contract outcome is a genuine win, and I think you structured it more intelligently than you might be giving yourself credit for. Let me break down why, and then get into the team perception question because that's the one that will require ongoing management.

On the package structure itself: Petrelli signed a two-year extension to October 2027, which gives you meaningful operational stability at a critical period. For a restaurant of your positioning in Higashi-Azabu, having a committed head chef through late 2027 means you can pursue longer-term goals — catering relationships, potential press attention, private dining expansion — without the shadow of a looming transition. The certainty that a signed two-year extension provides is worth something in itself, independent of the dollar figure.

The Petrelli new monthly base of 780,000 yen is substantial but defensible. For a trained Italian chef in Tokyo at a high-end trattoria, the competitive range for someone with a head chef role runs from roughly 650,000 to 900,000 yen depending on reputation and whether they're contributing to menu development and sourcing relationships. At 780,000, you're in the upper-middle of that range, which is appropriate if he's your primary creative driver and your operational anchor. What you did well is that you negotiated on the non-monetary terms rather than simply capping the base. The meal provision and transportation are real value to him at relatively low cost to you. The additional paid leave is the kind of benefit that builds loyalty without creating a recurring financial burden that scales with the business.

Now, team perception. The honest reality is that a 780,000 yen base is nearly double Nakajima's new 440,000. If that gap ever becomes visible — and in small teams, these things have a way of becoming partially visible even without anyone intending disclosure — you want to have a clear narrative ready. That narrative should emphasize specialization and market rate, not hierarchy for its own sake.

Yes — I want to talk about the part-time situation, specifically Yui Tachibana. She's been with us for about eighteen months, works four shifts a week, and she's become genuinely important to the front-of-house experience. Regulars ask for her by name, she handles wine service better than two of my full-timers, and she's discreet with VIP tables. I decided to reward that. Yui Tachibana raised to 1,500 yen per hour, up from 1,350. That's an 11 percent increase. I'm also thinking about how to retain her long-term because she's told me she's considering going full-time somewhere eventually. I don't want to lose her to a competitor just because I can't match a full-time package. Is there a middle ground I can offer her?

Yui Tachibana is exactly the kind of part-time staff member that restaurants lose unnecessarily, usually because owners treat hourly rate as the only lever available — and you've already moved the right direction there. Yui Tachibana raised to 1,500 yen per hour is a strong signal of recognition, and at that rate she's above the mid-tier Tokyo hospitality part-time range, which puts you in a competitive position against casual dining competitors. But you're right that hourly rate alone won't hold someone who is thinking about a full-time future, so let's think about what a meaningful middle-ground retention package actually looks like.

The first tool worth considering is a structured retention bonus. Given that she's at eighteen months now, a milestone payment that kicks in at the two-year mark gives her a concrete financial reason to stay through that point. The framing matters: this should feel like recognition of loyalty rather than a bribe to stay. A two-year retention bonus of 200,000 yen at 24 months is a number that's significant enough to matter to a part-time worker — it represents roughly four months of her additional earnings from the raise — but it's manageable for the business as a single payment rather than an ongoing liability. You could structure this as a lump sum paid on the anniversary of her hire date, contingent on continued employment at that point.

Beyond the bonus, think about what a full-time life would give her that her current arrangement doesn't: social insurance enrollment, paid leave accrual, a more stable monthly income figure, and a sense of career legitimacy that she can point to on a resume. Some of those things you can partially replicate. If she's working four shifts a week consistently, you may be approaching thresholds where she qualifies for partial social insurance enrollment depending on your hours and revenue structure — worth checking with your labor consultant.

I really like the retention bonus idea. I'm going to move forward with that — the two-year retention bonus: 200,000 yen at 24 months, exactly as you outlined. I want to make sure the conversation with her is framed correctly though. I don't want her to feel like she's being managed or manipulated. I also want to think through the remaining four full-time staff briefly — I haven't talked about them yet. The increases for that group were more modest, mostly in the 3 to 5 percent range, and one person received no increase at all. That last one is the conversation I'm most nervous about. How do I handle the no-increase situation without damaging the relationship or losing the person entirely?

Let me handle the Yui conversation framing first, and then we'll go straight into the no-increase situation because that one deserves careful thought.

For Yui: the key to making the retention bonus feel like recognition rather than manipulation is in the timing and language. Don't present it in the same breath as your concerns about her leaving. Instead, frame it as something you decided as part of a broader review of how you compensate people who have built genuine expertise in the restaurant — because that's the honest truth of what you did. Say something like: you've been here eighteen months, you've developed skills that directly affect the guest experience at our most important tables, and I want to make sure the way we compensate you reflects that trajectory. As part of your review, you want to introduce a milestone bonus at the two-year mark. Present the two-year retention bonus of 200,000 yen at 24 months as one component of a recognition package alongside the hourly increase you've already given her, not as a condition or a contract.

Now, the no-increase situation. The first principle: a zero increase is only sustainable if the employee understands specifically why, and specifically what would need to change for next year to be different. Vague language like 'this was a tough year' or 'we need to evaluate things' is worse than useless — it leaves the person with no agency and no pathway, which breeds resentment. You need to be able to say, concretely, what the performance gap is. Not in a punitive way, but in a factual one: here is what I observed, here is why it matters to the restaurant, and here is what a different outcome next year would look like.

The person is Takeda, one of my floor staff. He's been with me three years but this past year he's had multiple issues — late arrivals, a complaint from a regular about his attitude, and honestly his attention to table management has slipped. I've had informal conversations with him about it twice, but nothing formal or documented. He knows something is coming because everyone else on the team knows they're getting reviews this week. I'm worried that if he pushes back on the no-increase decision and mentions the previous informal conversations, I'm going to be in a weak position because I don't have a paper trail. How do I handle this from both a management and a legal standpoint?

This is the right question to be asking before the conversation, not after, so let's be direct about where you stand and what to do.

From a documentation standpoint, you are in a weaker position than you should be, and it's worth acknowledging that honestly so you don't walk into this conversation with false confidence. In Japanese labor law, dismissals and adverse employment actions are held to a relatively high standard of procedural fairness, and 'I told him informally twice' without any written record is not a strong foundation if Takeda decides to escalate. However — and this is important — you are not dismissing him. You are delivering a zero salary increase. That is a categorically different action. Withholding a raise is not a disciplinary sanction under Japanese labor law; it is a compensation decision, and employers have meaningful discretion in how they allocate compensation increases based on performance, as long as the decision is not discriminatory on protected grounds and not a violation of any contractual minimum.

That said, this conversation is the moment to create a paper trail, not a moment to be paralyzed by the absence of one. Here is how to structure it:

Begin by acknowledging his tenure — three years is real and should be named. Then transition into a candid but respectful account of what you've observed this year: the punctuality pattern, the customer complaint, the table management issues. You do not need to position these as allegations; you can present them as your own observations and the feedback you received. Then say directly: as a result of this review period, I am not in a position to offer a salary increase this year. That is the decision. State it clearly, without excessive softening, because hedging makes it worse.

Immediately after: give him a pathway. Tell him you want to be specific about what a different outcome looks like next year. Outline two or three concrete, observable behaviors — consistent punctuality over a six-month period, no further customer complaints about service attitude, demonstrable improvement in table turnover management. Tell him you want to do a formal check-in at the six-month mark to assess progress, and that you will document both today's conversation and that check-in.

Critically: after this meeting, write a brief internal memo to the file summarizing what was discussed, what was decided, and what the performance expectations are going forward.
